items.title: CPU governor for pinned KVM vCPUs
items.text:
The action in this article has been conducted under the following conditions:

Property Value Date September 2026 Kernel 6.8.0-139-generic Distribution Linux Mint 22.3 QEMU 8.2.2 libvirt 10.0.0

Related: Windows 11 Gaming VM with GPU pass-thru.
path: CPU governor for pinned KVM vCPUs

items.title: Problem
items.text:
Pinned guest vCPUs only stay on the host CPUs you assign. They do not get a performance frequency governor by themselves.

A common first step is a udev rule that sets scaling_governor=performance on those CPUs at ACTION=="add" (device appear at boot). That works on a quiet boot. After a Debian / Ubuntu / Linux Mint upgrade, the cpufrequtils LSB service typically starts next and writes ondemand (or whatever GOVERNOR is) to every CPU. The udev change is gone before login.

Confirm with:

cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu*/cpufreq/scaling_governor

If every line is ondemand even though the udev rule exists, this is the race.

This is not CPU isolation (isolcpus) and not systemd CPUAffinity. Those keep other tasks off the guest CPUs. The governor only controls how high those CPUs clock when they do run work.
path: CPU governor for pinned KVM vCPUs

items.title: Approach
items.text:
Keep the udev rule as a first attempt. Make the setting survive cpufrequtils with a oneshot unit that runs after it.

  • Host CPUs used by the desktop stay on ondemand (via cpufrequtils).
  • Host CPUs listed in the guest <cputune> / cpuset are forced to performance.

Example: a guest pinned to host CPUs 8-15 uses that same list here. Substitute the set from virsh vcpuinfo <domain> / the domain XML.
path: CPU governor for pinned KVM vCPUs

items.title: Host files
items.text:
The unit, helper, and defaults below are also in host/ in this repository. The optional udev rule is not. From a checkout:

sudo sh docs/research/VFIO/host/install.sh 8-15

Without the CPU-list argument the script only installs the sample VM_CPUS=8-15 file and does not enable the unit. Pass this host’s guest pin list to write it and systemctl enable --now. An existing /etc/default/cpufrequtils is left in place.
path: CPU governor for pinned KVM vCPUs

items.title: 1. CPU list
items.text:
/etc/default/vm-cpu-governor

# Host CPUs reserved for pinned KVM guests.
# Use the same set as <vcpu cpuset="..."> / <cputune><vcpupin>.
VM_CPUS=8-15
VM_GOVERNOR=performance
path: CPU governor for pinned KVM vCPUs

items.title: 2. Keep cpufrequtils from becoming a silent default
items.text:
/etc/default/cpufrequtils is optional but useful: the init script sources it if present. This keeps host-wide policy explicit after package upgrades.

ENABLE="true"
GOVERNOR="ondemand"
MAX_SPEED="0"
MIN_SPEED="0"

Leave ENABLE="true" so leftover host CPUs still get ondemand. Do not set GOVERNOR="performance" here unless you want the entire machine on that governor.
path: CPU governor for pinned KVM vCPUs

items.title: 3. Helper script
items.text:
/usr/local/sbin/set-vm-cpu-governor

#!/bin/sh
# Apply a cpufreq governor to the host CPUs reserved for pinned KVM guests.
set -eu

VM_CPUS=8-15
VM_GOVERNOR=performance

if [ -r /etc/default/vm-cpu-governor ]; then
    # shellcheck disable=SC1091
    . /etc/default/vm-cpu-governor
fi

expand_cpus() {
    echo "$1" | tr ',' '\n' | while IFS= read -r tok; do
        tok=$(printf '%s' "$tok" | tr -d '[:space:]')
        [ -z "$tok" ] && continue
        case "$tok" in
        *-*)
            start=${tok%-*}
            end=${tok#*-}
            seq "$start" "$end"
            ;;
        *)
            printf '%s\n' "$tok"
            ;;
        esac
    done
}

status=0
for cpu in $(expand_cpus "$VM_CPUS"); do
    gov="/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu${cpu}/cpufreq/scaling_governor"
    if [ ! -f "$gov" ]; then
        echo "set-vm-cpu-governor: missing $gov" >&2
        status=1
        continue
    fi
    printf '%s\n' "$VM_GOVERNOR" > "$gov"
done
exit "$status"

sudo chmod 755 /usr/local/sbin/set-vm-cpu-governor
path: CPU governor for pinned KVM vCPUs

items.title: 4. systemd oneshot
items.text:
/etc/systemd/system/vm-cpu-governor.service

[Unit]
Description=Set cpufreq governor on host CPUs reserved for KVM guests
After=cpufrequtils.service
After=loadcpufreq.service
Wants=loadcpufreq.service

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/local/sbin/set-vm-cpu-governor
RemainAfterExit=yes

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now vm-cpu-governor.service
path: CPU governor for pinned KVM vCPUs

items.title: 5. Optional udev rule (manual only)
items.text:
This rule is not in host/ and install.sh does not install it. Create the file by hand if you still want the boot-time first attempt. It is not sufficient on its own after cpufrequtils is installed.

/etc/udev/rules.d/90-scaling-governor-performance.rules

KERNEL=="cpu8|cpu9|cpu10|cpu11|cpu12|cpu13|cpu14|cpu15", SUBSYSTEM=="cpu", ACTION=="add", ATTR{cpufreq/scaling_governor}="performance"

Adjust the KERNEL== match if your guest CPU set is not 8-15.
path: CPU governor for pinned KVM vCPUs

items.title: Verify
items.text:
systemctl status vm-cpu-governor.service --no-pager
for i in $(seq 0 15); do
  printf 'cpu%-2s %s\n' "$i" "$(cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu$i/cpufreq/scaling_governor)"
done

Expected pattern on a 16-thread host with guests pinned to 8-15:

  • cpu0–cpu7: ondemand
  • cpu8–cpu15: performance

Re-check after a reboot. If everything is ondemand again, vm-cpu-governor.service is not enabled or After=cpufrequtils.service is missing.
path: CPU governor for pinned KVM vCPUs

items.title: Notes
items.text:
• Changing the governor does not pin QEMU threads. Keep <cputune> in the domain XML.
  • Keeping other host tasks off those CPUs is a separate step: Host CPU affinity for pinned VMs.
  • isolcpus= is a more aggressive option than slice AllowedCPUs=. It was left unused here.
  • On AMD Zen, Linux CPU numbers N and N+core_count are usually SMT siblings of the same physical core. Pin and governor lists should still match whatever you already chose in libvirt; this unit does not change that layout.
path: CPU governor for pinned KVM vCPUs

items.title: Guest CPU topology vs pin map
items.text:
The action in this article has been conducted under the following conditions:

Property Value Date September 2026 Kernel 6.8.0-139-generic Distribution Linux Mint 22.3 libvirt 10.0.0

Related: Windows 11 Gaming VM with GPU pass-thru.
path: Guest CPU topology vs pin map

items.title: Problem
items.text:
<cputune> says which host CPU each vCPU thread runs on. <cpu><topology> is what the guest OS believes.

Those two must describe the same shape. If they do not, Windows schedules as if some vCPUs were SMT siblings when they are not.

A common first pin on a 16-thread AMD host is:

<vcpu placement="static" cpuset="8-15">8</vcpu>

with one vCPU per host CPU 8 through 15. On Zen, those numbers are usually the second thread of eight different physical cores (0/8, 1/9, …), not four cores with two threads each.

Advertising this to the guest is then wrong:

<topology sockets="1" dies="1" cores="4" threads="2"/>

Windows will treat vCPU 0+1, 2+3, … as siblings. They are not.
path: Guest CPU topology vs pin map

items.title: Approach
items.text:
Keep the host pin list (8-15 or whatever you already chose). Change only the advertised topology so each vCPU is a full core with one thread:

<cpu mode="host-passthrough" check="none" migratable="on">
  <topology sockets="1" dies="1" cores="8" threads="1"/>
  <cache mode="passthrough"/>
  <feature policy="require" name="topoext"/>
</cpu>

topoext stays on so the guest still sees AMD topology extensions. This does not move QEMU threads and does not change hugepages, governors, or slice affinity.

Do not switch to cores="4" threads="2" unless the pin list is real SMT pairs, for example 4,12,5,13,6,14,7,15 on a 3700X CCD. That is a different layout.
path: Guest CPU topology vs pin map

items.title: Apply
items.text:
The running domain keeps the old topology until the guest is shut down and started again. virsh define updates the persistent XML immediately.

virsh dumpxml --inactive <domain> > /tmp/<domain>.xml

Edit the <topology> line, then:

virsh define /tmp/<domain>.xml

Confirm:

virsh dumpxml --inactive <domain> | grep -A4 '<cpu '

After the next guest power cycle:

virsh dumpxml <domain> | grep topology

Inside Windows, Task Manager should show 8 cores / 8 logical processors, not 4 cores / 8 logical processors.
path: Guest CPU topology vs pin map

items.title: Notes
items.text:
• Same logical CPU count (8) so this is not a vCPU resize.
  • Leave <vcpupin> as-is when only fixing the advertised shape.
  • migratable="on" is unrelated; it can stay.
path: Guest CPU topology vs pin map

items.title: Host CPU affinity for pinned VMs
items.text:
The action in this article has been conducted under the following conditions:

Property Value Date September 2026 Kernel 6.8.0-139-generic Distribution Linux Mint 22.3 systemd 255 libvirt 10.0.0

Related:

  • Windows 11 Gaming VM with GPU pass-thru
  • CPU governor for pinned KVM vCPUs
path: Host CPU affinity for pinned VMs

items.title: Problem
items.text:
<cputune> only pins QEMU's vCPU threads. Everything else on the host (desktop session, browsers, Docker, libvirtd itself) can still run on those same host CPUs.

isolcpus= removes those CPUs from the general scheduler. It works, but it is a kernel cmdline change, needs a reboot, and can hurt host latency if you guessed wrong. The 2024 notes left it as an experiment.

On a cgroup v2 host, systemd slices are a milder way to get the same split.
path: Host CPU affinity for pinned VMs

items.title: Approach
items.text:
libvirt places QEMU in machine.slice (machine-qemu-*.scope). Keep that slice on every CPU so <vcpupin> can still target the guest set.

Put host userspace in the other two top-level slices:

Slice Typical members Allowed CPUs user.slice graphical session, terminals, browsers host set (example: 0-7) system.slice libvirtd, Docker, irqbalance host set (example: 0-7) machine.slice QEMU, swtpm, guest virtiofsd all CPUs (do not restrict)

Do not set CPUAffinity= on PID 1 in system.conf. That mask is inherited by everything systemd starts. A guest pinned to CPUs outside that mask may fail to run there.

This is not the performance governor. Governor and affinity solve different problems; use both.

Example split for a 16-thread host with guests pinned to 8-15: host slices get 0-7. Substitute the complement of your domain cpuset.
path: Host CPU affinity for pinned VMs

items.title: Host files
items.text:
The snippets below are also in host/ in this repository. From a checkout:

sudo sh docs/research/VFIO/host/install-host-affinity.sh

Reruns keep an existing /etc/default/vm-host-cpus so a custom HOST_CPUS is not replaced by the sample.

systemctl set-property applies the limit immediately. A reboot is not required, but it is the cleanest way to make sure every existing process picked it up.
path: Host CPU affinity for pinned VMs

items.title: 1. CPU list
items.text:
/etc/default/vm-host-cpus

# Host CPUs for user.slice and system.slice.
# Use the complement of the guest <vcpu cpuset="...">.
HOST_CPUS=0-7
path: Host CPU affinity for pinned VMs

items.title: 2. user.slice
items.text:
/etc/systemd/system/user.slice.d/50-host-cpus.conf

[Slice]
AllowedCPUs=0-7
path: Host CPU affinity for pinned VMs

items.title: 3. system.slice
items.text:
/etc/systemd/system/system.slice.d/50-host-cpus.conf

[Slice]
AllowedCPUs=0-7

Leave machine.slice without an AllowedCPUs= drop-in.

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl set-property --runtime user.slice AllowedCPUs=0-7
sudo systemctl set-property --runtime system.slice AllowedCPUs=0-7

--runtime applies the limit now. The drop-ins above are what survive a reboot. Omit --runtime only if you want systemd to write a second persistent file.
path: Host CPU affinity for pinned VMs

items.title: Verify
items.text:
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/user.slice/cpuset.cpus.effective
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/cpuset.cpus.effective
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/machine.slice/cpuset.cpus.effective

Expected on a 16-thread host with guests on 8-15:

  • user.slice / system.slice: 0-7
  • machine.slice: 0-15
# desktop / host services should stay on the host set
taskset -cp "$(pgrep -n Xorg)"
taskset -cp "$(pgrep -n libvirtd)"

# guest vCPU threads should still match <vcpupin>
for tid in /proc/$(pgrep -n qemu-system-x86_64)/task/*; do
  comm=$(cat "$tid/comm")
  case "$comm" in
    CPU*) printf '%s %s\n' "$comm" "$(taskset -cp "$(basename "$tid")" | sed 's/.*: //')" ;;
  esac
done

If vCPU threads suddenly show 0-7, machine.slice was restricted as well. Remove that drop-in and restart the guest.
path: Host CPU affinity for pinned VMs

items.title: Notes
items.text:
• irqbalance should still use IRQBALANCE_BANNED_CPULIST for the guest CPUs. Affinity does not replace that.
  • Kernel threads and init.scope are not in user.slice / system.slice. A few IRQs or kworkers may still appear on the guest CPUs.
  • isolcpus= remains optional. If you enable it later, keep the slice limits; they document the same split for userspace.
path: Host CPU affinity for pinned VMs

items.title: Looking Glass B7 with IVSHMEM
items.text:
The action in this article has been conducted under the following conditions:

Property Value Date September 2026 (updated November 2026) Kernel 6.8.0-139-generic Distribution Linux Mint 22.3 Mesa 25.2.8 (radeonsi) QEMU 8.2.2 libvirt 10.0.0 Looking Glass B7 (27fe47cb, 2025-03-06) kvmfr 0.0.9 (DKMS)

Official docs: libvirt/QEMU, kvmfr, Windows host, Linux client. Related: Windows 11 Gaming VM with GPU pass-thru.

items.title: Problem
items.text:
A VFIO Windows guest paints on the passed-through GPU. The host cannot see that framebuffer through Spice or virt-manager. Looking Glass copies frames over IVSHMEM so the Linux desktop can display the guest with low latency.

The Ubuntu / Mint looking-glass-client package is B6. The Windows host installer and the Linux client must be the same stable version. B7 is current stable.

Do not run two domains against the same IVSHMEM file (or the same GPU) at once.

Rust virtiofsd 1.10 (Ubuntu / Mint 22) dies with Illegal seek / vhost_set_mem_table failed if the domain also maps /dev/kvmfr0. That char device is not seekable, so the daemon exits and the guest share disappears. Use standard /dev/shm IVSHMEM on any guest that also has virtiofs. Keep kvmfr for domains that do not use virtiofs.

items.title: Host: shared memory
items.text:
Looking Glass requires a power-of-2 IVSHMEM size large enough for double-buffered frames plus header and cursor metadata:

IVSHMEM size Max resolution (SDR, 32-bit) Max resolution (HDR, 16-bit float) 32 MiB 1920×1080 — 64 MiB 2560×1440 1920×1080 128 MiB 3840×2160 (4K) 2560×1440 256 MiB 5120×2880+ 3840×2160 (4K)

Use 128 MiB if you want 1440p HDR or 4K SDR headroom without re-editing the XML later. Keep the <shmem> size identical across every domain that shares /dev/shm/looking-glass, and apply the change with a full domain shutdown and start (not an in-guest reboot).

Resizing an existing /dev/shm/looking-glass file

QEMU only sizes an empty (0-byte) backing file automatically. If /dev/shm/looking-glass still has the previous size (for example 32 MiB from an earlier boot), starting the domain fails with backing store size 0x2000000 does not match 'size' option 0x8000000. Shut down every domain that uses /dev/shm/looking-glass and close looking-glass-client before resetting the file to 0 bytes, then start the domain:

truncate -s 0 /dev/shm/looking-glass

# /etc/tmpfiles.d/10-looking-glass.conf
f /dev/shm/looking-glass 0660 <user> kvm -

sudo systemd-tmpfiles --create /etc/tmpfiles.d/10-looking-glass.conf

If AppArmor is enforcing, allow /dev/shm/looking-glass rw, in /etc/apparmor.d/local/abstractions/libvirt-qemu.

items.title: Domain XML
items.text:
Keep Spice for input and clipboard, drop the emulated QXL head (passthrough GPU is the only display), drop the USB tablet, and add virtio keyboard/mouse. Use libvirt <shmem>, not a qemu:commandline kvmfr backend.

<domain type="kvm">
  <!-- … -->
  <channel type="spicevmc">
    <target type="virtio" name="com.redhat.spice.0"/>
  </channel>
  <input type="mouse" bus="ps2"/>
  <input type="keyboard" bus="ps2"/>
  <input type="mouse" bus="virtio"/>
  <input type="keyboard" bus="virtio"/>
  <graphics type="spice" autoport="yes">
    <listen type="address"/>
    <image compression="off"/>
    <gl enable="no"/>
  </graphics>
  <sound model="ich9">
    <audio id="1"/>
  </sound>
  <audio id="1" type="spice"/>
  <video>
    <model type="none"/>
  </video>
  <shmem name="looking-glass">
    <model type="ivshmem-plain"/>
    <size unit="M">128</size>
  </shmem>
  <memballoon model="none"/>
</domain>

virsh define the inactive XML. virt-manager’s console will be blank after video none; that is expected.

items.title: Linux client (B7 from source)
items.text:
Download the stable source artifact from looking-glass.io/downloads, not apt install looking-glass-client.

mkdir -p client/build
cmake -S client -B client/build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX="$HOME/.local"
cmake --build client/build -j"$(nproc)"
cmake --install client/build
looking-glass-client --help   # banner: Looking Glass (B7)

B7 defaults app:shmFile to /dev/kvmfr0. Point it at the shm file instead. The client does not save the last window position; win:position is only the startup coordinate (center or <left>x<top>).

# ~/.config/looking-glass/client.ini
[app]
shmFile=/dev/shm/looking-glass

[win]
size=1920x1080
position=2112x180
autoResize=no
fullScreen=no
maximize=no
borderless=no

[input]
grabKeyboardOnFocus=yes
ignoreWindowsKeys=no

[egl]
preset=Upscaling

win:position is <left>x<top> in the combined desktop. 0x0 plus 1920x1080 fills a 1080p output and the window manager treats that as fullscreen. The values above park a 1080p window on a 2560×1440 display at +1920+0. win:autoResize=yes follows the guest framebuffer, not a fixed 1080p.

input:grabKeyboardOnFocus sends host combos such as Win+R into the guest as soon as the Looking Glass window has keyboard focus (no Scroll Lock). ignoreWindowsKeys=no is the default and must stay off. Hover alone is not enough on a click-to-focus desktop; enable sloppy/mouse focus in the window manager if the pointer entering the window should grab keys. Leave input:captureOnFocus off unless the mouse should lock into the window on focus.

egl:preset loads a saved EGL filter preset from ~/.config/looking-glass/presets/ automatically at startup (the client otherwise starts with no preset loaded). Create the preset through the overlay (Right Ctrl+O or Scroll Lock+O → EGL Filters → Save preset as…) instead of hand-editing files under presets/.

items.title: EGL upscaling (FSR1) black screen on Mesa 25.x
Symptom
items.text:
• AMD FidelityFX FSR: works while the client window is at or below the guest resolution (because ffxFSR1 is bypassed when no upscaling is needed), then turns the rendered image solid black the moment the window grows larger than the guest framebuffer.
  • AMD FidelityFX CAS: runs at any resolution without an upscaling check, so enabling it turns the rendered image solid black immediately regardless of window size.

items.title: Cause
items.text:
Looking Glass B7 (27fe47cb, 2025-03-06) compiles its EGL post-processing shaders as GLSL ES 3.00 (#version 300 es) with precision highp float; only, leaving int and uint at GLSL ES's default mediump (16-bit). Mesa 25.x on the host AMD GPU (radeonsi, here the RX 6900 XT driving the Linux client) began honoring 16-bit mediump int in fragment shaders (Mesa #12990). This is independent of the guest GPU (NVIDIA or AMD).

AMD FidelityFX FSR1 (ffx_fsr1_easu.frag, ffx_fsr1_rcas.frag) and CAS (ffx_cas.frag) pass packed 32-bit IEEE-754 float parameters through uvec4 uConsts and unpack them with 32-bit integer operations. Truncating those constants to 16-bit zeroes or corrupts them, producing a black frame.

items.title: Fix
items.text:
Apply upstream commit gnif/LookingGlass@60d7c849 ([client] egl: make int highp in fragment shaders) to the B7 source tree before building. Patching B7 instead of switching the client to master keeps protocol compatibility with the stable B7 Windows host service.

curl -fL "https://looking-glass.io/artifact/B7/source" -o looking-glass-B7.tar.gz
tar xzf looking-glass-B7.tar.gz
cd looking-glass-B7
curl -fL "https://github.com/gnif/LookingGlass/commit/60d7c849723ba9d044388d00e9a12ede056ff8de.patch" \
  -o highp-int.patch
# Skip the AUTHORS hunk (line numbers differ on B7) and apply only the EGL shader hunks
awk '/^diff --git /{skip=($0 ~ /AUTHORS$/)} !skip' highp-int.patch | patch -p1

cmake -S client -B client/build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX="$HOME/.local"
cmake --build client/build -j"$(nproc)"

Verify that the compiled binary contains precision highp int; in all 11 fragment shaders, then install it atomically (overwriting a running binary in place fails with ETXTBSY):

strings client/build/looking-glass-client | grep -c "precision highp int;"   # expected: 11
install -m 0755 client/build/looking-glass-client "$HOME/.local/bin/looking-glass-client.new"
mv -f "$HOME/.local/bin/looking-glass-client.new" "$HOME/.local/bin/looking-glass-client"

Relaunch looking-glass-client, enable AMD FidelityFX FSR in the EGL Filters tab, save a preset (for example Upscaling), and reference it via [egl] preset=Upscaling in ~/.config/looking-glass/client.ini.

Native resolution vs. host-side FSR1

Host-side FSR 1.0 is purely spatial, so raising IVSHMEM to 64 or 128 MiB and running the guest at native monitor resolution still produces sharper desktop text and lets games use temporal upscalers (DLSS, FSR 2+, XeSS). Keep the FSR1 preset enabled as a fallback: it remains inactive when the captured frame matches the client output and activates only when the guest framebuffer (for example, a lower-resolution fullscreen mode) or an earlier filter's output (such as the Downscaler filter) is smaller than the client output. A smaller game window inside a native-resolution guest desktop does not reduce the captured frame size.

items.title: Windows host (B7)
items.text:
1. Start the domain so the new IVSHMEM device is present.
  2. Copy looking-glass-host-setup.exe from the B7 Windows Host artifact into the guest (virtiofs or ISO).
  3. Run the installer as Administrator. Since B6 the installer ships the IVSHMEM driver.
  4. Install the virtio input driver (vioinput) from virtio-win if Device Manager shows unknown keyboard/mouse devices.
  5. Optional clipboard: Spice guest tools, with the com.redhat.spice.0 channel above.

Host log on failure: %ProgramData%\Looking Glass (host)\looking-glass-host.txt.

items.title: Guest needs a display sink
items.text:
NVIDIA and post-GCN AMD GPUs power down the display block when nothing is plugged in. DXGI then has no desktop to capture, so the Linux client stays on the splash / blank even though both Looking Glass processes are running.

video none plus GPU passthrough does not count as a monitor. Attach a real display to the guest GPU, or a DisplayPort/HDMI dummy plug. This guest uses an HDMI dummy on the passed-through RTX 2080 SUPER. After the sink appears, restart the Looking Glass host service (or reboot the guest) and reopen the client.

Stable B7 has no Indirect Display Driver. Bleeding-edge builds ship a Windows IDD if you want a virtual sink later.

items.title: Run
items.text:
looking-glass-client

If the client says it is waiting for the host, the Windows service is not running or IVSHMEM is missing. If both ends are running but the picture is still empty, check the guest GPU has a sink. If the picture is cropped at the bottom, the IVSHMEM size is too small for that resolution.

If virtiofs dies with Illegal seek / vhost_set_mem_table failed, the domain is still mapping /dev/kvmfr0. Remove the kvmfr qemu:commandline block.

items.title: Raw virtio-blk boot disk
items.text:
The action in this article has been conducted under the following conditions:

Property Value Date September 2026 Kernel 6.8.0-139-generic Distribution Linux Mint 22.3 QEMU 8.2.2 libvirt 10.0.0

Related: Windows 11 Gaming VM with GPU pass-thru.

items.title: Problem
items.text:
A Windows guest installed on emulated SATA (ide-hd) with a qcow2 system disk spends a lot of I/O time in QEMU even when the file lives on a fast NVMe. Two leftover iothreads do nothing if no disk references them.

VirtIO block (viostor) is the usual driver if the guest already has extra virtio-blk data disks. VirtIO SCSI (vioscsi) is a different driver; switching the boot disk to SCSI in the same window can fail to boot unless that driver is already a Boot-start device.

items.title: Approach
items.text:
In one downtime window:

  1. Confirm viostor is Boot and Running in the guest (driverquery / pnputil).
  2. Shut the domain down (not reboot).
  3. Convert the system qcow2 to raw next to the original. Keep the qcow2 until Windows has booted cleanly.
  4. Point the persistent XML at the raw file as virtio-blk with an iothread.
<disk type="file" device="disk">
  <driver name="qemu" type="raw" cache="none" io="io_uring" discard="unmap" iothread="1"/>
  <source file="/var/lib/libvirt/images/guest-system.raw"/>
  <target dev="vde" bus="virtio"/>
  <boot order="1"/>
</disk>

target dev must be an unused virtio name. List existing ones before you edit:

virsh dumpxml --inactive <domain> | grep -E "bus=.virtio"

If vda–vdd are already data disks (or other virtio devices), pick the next free vdX (vde in the example). Leave those disks and GPU hostdevs unchanged. Omit <address> on the new disk so libvirt picks a free PCIe port.

Have BitLocker recovery material reachable. A controller change can demand it.

items.title: Convert
items.text:
The domain must be shut off. Run the convert as root, then give the image back to the qemu user:

sudo qemu-img convert -p -f qcow2 -O raw \
  /var/lib/libvirt/images/guest-system.qcow2 \
  /var/lib/libvirt/images/guest-system.raw
sudo chown libvirt-qemu:kvm /var/lib/libvirt/images/guest-system.raw
sudo chmod 600 /var/lib/libvirt/images/guest-system.raw
sudo qemu-img info /var/lib/libvirt/images/guest-system.raw

Need enough free space for the raw file plus the qcow2 until you delete the old one.

items.title: Define and start
items.text:
virsh dumpxml --inactive <domain> > /tmp/<domain>.xml
cp /tmp/<domain>.xml /tmp/<domain>.rollback.xml
# edit /tmp/<domain>.xml (the system <disk> as above)
virsh define /tmp/<domain>.xml
virsh start <domain>

If Windows does not boot on the raw virtio-blk disk, define the rollback XML and start again. The qcow2 is still the boot image in that file:

virsh destroy <domain>   # only if it is still running
virsh define /tmp/<domain>.rollback.xml
virsh start <domain>

Confirm:

virsh dumpxml <domain> | grep -A8 "device='disk'"

The boot disk should show type='raw', bus='virtio', and iothread='1'.

Inside Windows, the boot volume should appear as a Red Hat VirtIO disk (VEN_1AF4&DEV_1042) with viostor still Boot/Running.

items.title: Retire the qcow2
items.text: Keep the qcow2 until the guest has completed two clean boots. Then rename or delete it. Do not delete it to “free space” on the first attempt.

items.title: Secondary virtio-blk data disks
items.text:
If the domain already defines a second pinned IOThread (such as <iothreadpin iothread="2" cpuset="2-3"/>), apply the same io_uring and discard="unmap" driver flags to any dedicated block data disk (for example, a passed-through SATA SSD for games):

<disk type="block" device="disk">
  <driver name="qemu" type="raw" cache="none" io="io_uring" discard="unmap" iothread="2"/>
  <source dev="/dev/sdX"/>
  <target dev="vdc" bus="virtio"/>
</disk>

Define the updated inactive XML and perform a full domain shutdown and start so QEMU applies the new driver parameters.

items.title: Notes
items.text:
• This is not virtio-scsi. Use SCSI only after vioscsi is a Boot-start driver.
  • io='io_uring' needs a recent QEMU and kernel (8.2 / 6.8 here).
  • Reuse the same recipe on other Windows domains that already have viostor in use.

items.title: Windows 11 Gaming VM with GPU pass-thru
items.text:
Property Value Date November 2026 Kernel 6.8.0-139-generic Distribution Linux Mint 22.3 QEMU 8.2.2 libvirt 10.0.0 Guest OS Windows 11 25H2 (build 26200)

Related: Looking Glass B7 with IVSHMEM, Guest CPU topology vs pin map, CPU governor for pinned KVM vCPUs, Host CPU affinity for pinned VMs, Raw virtio-blk boot disk, Debugging Windows 11 guest stalls.
path: Windows 11 Gaming VM with GPU pass-thru

items.title: Hardware
items.text:
Part Role Device Mainboard Host ASUS ROG Crosshair VIII Hero (BIOS 4805) CPU Host and guest AMD Ryzen 7 3700X (8 cores / 16 threads) Memory Host 64 GiB (24 GiB reserved as static 2 MiB hugepages for the guest) GPU Host display AMD Radeon RX 6900 XT (16 GB) GPU Guest (VFIO) NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 SUPER (8 GB) Storage Host OS WD Black SN850X 2 TB NVMe Storage Guest system disk WD Black SN850X 2 TB NVMe (raw virtio-blk image) Storage Guest games disk Samsung SSD 870 EVO 2 TB (raw virtio-blk block device) USB Optional guest passthrough VIA VL805/VL806 SuperSpeed USB 3.0 host controller

Two GPUs are required. The host keeps the RX 6900 XT. The RTX 2080 SUPER and its extra functions go to the guest.
path: Windows 11 Gaming VM with GPU pass-thru

items.title: Host kernel
items.text:
Bind the guest GPU functions to vfio-pci and reserve hugepages before QEMU starts. PCI BDFs move if the card changes slot; the IDs do not.

GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT="... vfio-pci.ids=10de:1e81,10de:10f8,10de:1ad8,10de:1ad9 kvm.ignore_msrs=1 hugepages=12288 video=efifb:off video=vesafb:off video=simplefb:off"

12288 pages of 2 MiB is 24 GiB. Confirm page size with grep Hugepagesize /proc/meminfo. The video=…fb:off flags keep the host firmware framebuffer off the NVIDIA card so it is free for VFIO.

Load VFIO early:

# /etc/modules-load.d/vfio.conf
vfio
vfio_pci
vfio_iommu_type1
vfio_virqfd

Blacklist host NVIDIA drivers so they never bind the guest GPU. Libvirt managed="yes" then attaches vfio-pci when the domain starts:

# /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-nouveau.conf
blacklist nouveau
options nouveau modeset=0

# /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-nvidia.conf
blacklist nvidia
blacklist nvidia_drm
blacklist nvidia_modeset
blacklist nvidia_uvm
blacklist nvidia-peermem

nvidiafb stays in the distribution blacklist-framebuffer.conf.

/etc/sysctl.conf:

kernel.shmmax = 25769803776
vm.nr_hugepages = 12288
vm.min_free_kbytes = 112640
vm.hugetlb_shm_group = 1000

hugetlb_shm_group is the desktop user’s gid so QEMU can use the pool.
path: Windows 11 Gaming VM with GPU pass-thru

items.title: Guest GPU (VFIO)
items.text:
TU104 exposes four functions. They share IOMMU group 32, so pass all of them. On this machine they sit at 0d:00.0–0d:00.3:

0d:00.0 VGA compatible controller [10de:1e81]  TU104 (RTX 2080 SUPER)
0d:00.1 Audio device             [10de:10f8]  HD Audio
0d:00.2 USB controller           [10de:1ad8]  USB 3.1 xHCI
0d:00.3 Serial bus controller    [10de:1ad9]  USB Type-C UCSI

The full group list is in IOMMU dump. Looking Glass needs an active display sink on this GPU; this guest uses an HDMI dummy plug. See Looking Glass B7.
path: Windows 11 Gaming VM with GPU pass-thru

items.title: Input and USB passthrough
items.text:
Daily keyboard, mouse, and clipboard go over Looking Glass plus Spice. The domain has a com.redhat.spice.0 channel and virtio keyboard/mouse (vioinput in Windows). That is enough for the Linux desktop to drive the guest; a dedicated PCI USB controller is not attached.

The guest still receives the RTX 2080 SUPER’s own USB-C controller (0d:00.2 and 0d:00.3) because those functions live in the same IOMMU group as the GPU.
path: Windows 11 Gaming VM with GPU pass-thru

items.title: Optional: dedicated USB controller passthrough
items.text:
A whole xHCI controller can still go to the guest so physical keyboard and mouse devices never share the host. Two controllers on this board are in their own resettable groups:

Controller PCI ID BDF IOMMU group VIA VL805/VL806 add-in card 1106:3483 05:00.0 24 CPU Matisse USB 3.0 1022:149c 0f:00.3 36

The chipset Matisse controllers at 07:00.1 and 07:00.3 share group 20 with the Starship/Matisse Reserved SPP device, so they are a poor passthrough target.

This host currently leaves both isolated controllers on xhci_hcd. Remaining host USB includes the VIA card, the rear Matisse hub (AURA, headset, Bluetooth, Keychron Link), and the Cooler Master ARES plus OBSBOT camera on the 6900 XT’s own USB.
path: Windows 11 Gaming VM with GPU pass-thru

items.title: Domain CPU and memory
items.text:
Pin the guest to host CPUs 8-15. Leave 0-7 for the desktop. Those eight host CPUs are not four SMT pairs, so the guest topology is 8 cores / 1 thread. cores=4 threads=2 does not match this pin map. See Guest CPU topology vs pin map.

Give the guest 24 GiB of hugepage-backed RAM to match hugepages=12288. The system disk is raw virtio-blk with io_uring; a dedicated SATA SSD is a second virtio-blk disk on IOThread 2. Recipe: Raw virtio-blk boot disk.

<memory unit="KiB">25165824</memory>
<currentMemory unit="KiB">25165824</currentMemory>
<vcpu placement="static" cpuset="8-15">8</vcpu>
<iothreads>2</iothreads>
<cputune>
  <vcpupin vcpu="0" cpuset="8"/>
  <vcpupin vcpu="1" cpuset="9"/>
  <vcpupin vcpu="2" cpuset="10"/>
  <vcpupin vcpu="3" cpuset="11"/>
  <vcpupin vcpu="4" cpuset="12"/>
  <vcpupin vcpu="5" cpuset="13"/>
  <vcpupin vcpu="6" cpuset="14"/>
  <vcpupin vcpu="7" cpuset="15"/>
  <emulatorpin cpuset="0-1"/>
  <iothreadpin iothread="1" cpuset="0-1"/>
  <iothreadpin iothread="2" cpuset="2-3"/>
</cputune>

<cpu mode="host-passthrough" check="none" migratable="on">
  <topology sockets="1" dies="1" cores="8" threads="1"/>
  <cache mode="passthrough"/>
  <feature policy="require" name="topoext"/>
</cpu>

<memoryBacking>
  <hugepages>
    <page size="2048" unit="KiB"/>
  </hugepages>
  <access mode="shared"/>
</memoryBacking>

Hide KVM from the NVIDIA Windows driver (Code 43) and keep the Hyper-V enlightenments Windows 11 expects:

<features>
  <hyperv mode="custom">
    <relaxed state="on"/>
    <vapic state="on"/>
    <spinlocks state="on" retries="8191"/>
    <vpindex state="on"/>
    <runtime state="on"/>
    <synic state="on"/>
    <stimer state="on">
      <direct state="on"/>
    </stimer>
    <reset state="on"/>
    <vendor_id state="on" value="0123456789ab"/>
    <frequencies state="on"/>
    <reenlightenment state="on"/>
    <tlbflush state="on"/>
    <ipi state="on"/>
    <evmcs state="off"/>
  </hyperv>
  <kvm>
    <hidden state="on"/>
  </kvm>
</features>

Windows 11 boots from OVMF (OVMF_CODE_4M.secboot.fd) with an emulated TPM 2.0. secure-boot is on but enrolled-keys is off and the NVRAM template is empty OVMF_VARS_4M.fd, so firmware does not enforce signatures and Windows reports Secure Boot as off. Leave that as-is on this guest: regenerating NVRAM would wipe existing EFI variables. A new VM that needs enforcement should set enrolled-keys to yes and use OVMF_VARS_4M.ms.fd. The clock uses local time with a native TSC and Hyper-V clock:

<os firmware="efi">
  <type arch="x86_64" machine="pc-q35-6.2">hvm</type>
  <firmware>
    <feature enabled="no" name="enrolled-keys"/>
    <feature enabled="yes" name="secure-boot"/>
  </firmware>
  <loader readonly="yes" secure="yes" type="pflash">/usr/share/OVMF/OVMF_CODE_4M.secboot.fd</loader>
  <nvram template="/usr/share/OVMF/OVMF_VARS_4M.fd"/>
</os>

<tpm model="tpm-crb">
  <backend type="emulator" version="2.0"/>
</tpm>

<clock offset="localtime">
  <timer name="rtc" tickpolicy="catchup"/>
  <timer name="pit" tickpolicy="delay"/>
  <timer name="hpet" present="no"/>
  <timer name="hypervclock" present="yes"/>
  <timer name="tsc" present="yes" mode="native"/>
</clock>

access mode=shared is required for virtiofs. On Mint 22, rust virtiofsd 1.10 cannot share a domain with /dev/kvmfr0 (Illegal seek). Looking Glass on a virtiofs guest must use /dev/shm — see Looking Glass B7.

Spice stays for input. Do not add a QXL head when the RTX 2080 SUPER is the only display.
path: Windows 11 Gaming VM with GPU pass-thru

items.title: Host CPU tuning
items.text:
Keep host CPUs 8-15 on performance so pinned vCPUs can clock up. A udev rule on ACTION=="add" is the first step:

echo 'KERNEL=="cpu8|cpu9|cpu10|cpu11|cpu12|cpu13|cpu14|cpu15", SUBSYSTEM=="cpu", ACTION=="add", ATTR{cpufreq/scaling_governor}="performance"' | sudo tee /etc/udev/rules.d/90-scaling-governor-performance.rules

After a Debian / Mint upgrade, cpufrequtils may start later and write ondemand to every CPU. Confirm with cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu*/cpufreq/scaling_governor. If everything is ondemand, the udev rule lost the race. Restore performance on the pinned CPUs with the oneshot in CPU governor for pinned KVM vCPUs.

Keep host IRQs off the guest CPUs:

# /etc/default/irqbalance
IRQBALANCE_BANNED_CPULIST=8-15

sudo systemctl restart irqbalance

isolcpus=8-15 was tried and not proven better. Leave it off unless you re-test host and guest together. Prefer systemd slice AllowedCPUs= so host userspace stays off the guest CPUs without a kernel cmdline change: Host CPU affinity for pinned VMs.
path: Windows 11 Gaming VM with GPU pass-thru

items.title: Bridge
items.text:
One way to put the guest on the LAN is a oneshot that builds br0 on the I211 (04:d9:f5:60:f0:0a). Adding the VIA USB card renamed that NIC from enp5s0 to enp6s0, so the unit selects the NIC by MAC instead of interface name. Match that MAC only on a physical netdev (/sys/class/net/<iface>/device) so br0 cannot steal the lookup if it later copies the port MAC. Create br0 only if it is missing, and attach the I211 only if it is not already a member. Any other brctl failure still fails the unit so Restart=on-failure can run:

# /lib/systemd/system/qemu-startup.service
[Unit]
Description=Setup qemu network bridging
After=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=oneshot
Restart=on-failure
ExecStart=/bin/sh -c '[ -d /sys/class/net/br0 ] || brctl addbr br0'
ExecStart=/bin/sh -c 'nic=$(ip -o link | awk -F": " "/04:d9:f5:60:f0:0a/{print \\$2}" | while read i; do [ -e /sys/class/net/$i/device ] && echo "$i" && break; done); [ -n "$nic" ] || exit 1; [ -e /sys/class/net/br0/brif/"$nic" ] || brctl addif br0 "$nic"'
ExecStart=dhclient br0
ExecStart=ip link set br0 up
ExecStart=iptables -I FORWARD -m physdev --physdev-is-bridged -j ACCEPT

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

sudo systemctl enable --now qemu-startup.service

The guest NIC is virtio on that bridge.

items.title: Debugging Windows 11 guest stalls that look like slow disk I/O
items.text:
The investigation in this article was conducted under the following conditions:

Property Value Date November 2026 Host kernel 6.8.0-139-generic Host distribution Linux Mint 22.3 QEMU 8.2.2 libvirt 10.0.0 virtiofsd 1.10.0 Guest OS Windows 11 25H2 (build 26200, stripped custom image)

Related: Windows 11 Gaming VM with GPU pass-thru, Looking Glass B7 with IVSHMEM, Raw virtio-blk boot disk.
path: Debugging Windows 11 guest stalls that look like slow disk I/O

items.title: Problem
items.text:
A Windows 11 VFIO guest booted quickly and showed low CPU, RAM, and disk utilization, yet interactive workloads stalled severely:

  • Launching PowerShell 7 took minutes while loading assemblies.
  • File Explorer (This PC, Run) hung indefinitely.
  • Downloads and network tools paused for ~24 seconds before transferring data.
  • Small .msi installers took 20–30+ minutes or timed out.

The symptoms looked like failing virtual storage or KVM thread contention. Measuring completed host block I/O ruled out slow completed disk transfers first; the stalls turned out to be four independent bottlenecks stacked on top of each other across VirtIO-FS, leftover Defender drivers, LAN IPv6 DNS, and Windows 11 24H2/25H2 Smart App Control Evaluation Mode, plus a missing SPICE channel blocking spice-vdagent.
path: Debugging Windows 11 guest stalls that look like slow disk I/O

items.title: 1. Rule out host storage and KVM
items.text:
Before changing guest storage or CPU tuning, measure actual block-device latency from QEMU via QMP so you know whether completed I/O is stalling below or inside Windows.

List the domain's block devices first to find each disk's QMP qdev device ID (such as virtio-disk0 and virtio-disk1):

virsh qemu-monitor-command <domain> '{"execute":"query-block"}'

Enable latency histograms on every disk under test:

for id in virtio-disk0 virtio-disk1; do
  virsh qemu-monitor-command <domain> \
    "{\"execute\":\"block-latency-histogram-set\",\"arguments\":{\"id\":\"$id\",\"boundaries\":[1000000,5000000,20000000,100000000]}}"
done

Trigger a stall in the guest, then query counters and histograms:

virsh qemu-monitor-command <domain> '{"execute":"query-blockstats"}'

On this guest, both virtio-blk disks averaged ~115 µs per read and ~88 µs per write, with zero I/Os ≥ 20 ms across ~172,000 operations, zero failed I/Os, and 0% disk busy during hangs. Inside Windows, a 500× 4 KiB write/read/delete loop finished in 150–290 ms and copying + executing whoami.exe took ~25 ms.

Looking Glass and virtiofsd

virtiofsd 1.10 exits with Illegal seek if the domain also maps /dev/kvmfr0 (see Looking Glass B7 with IVSHMEM). This guest already used /dev/shm/looking-glass, so Looking Glass was not crashing virtiofsd.

With completed host I/O fast, the remaining stalls appeared to lie in software layers above the disk. QEMU latency histograms record only completed or failed requests, so they do not by themselves exclude a request that remains outstanding in flight during a hang.
path: Debugging Windows 11 guest stalls that look like slow disk I/O

items.title: 2. Wedged VirtIO-FS / WinFsp mount
path: Debugging Windows 11 guest stalls that look like slow disk I/O

items.title: Symptom
items.text:
• PowerShell 7 hung for minutes on startup and eventually printed:
Attempting to perform the InitializeDefaultDrives operation on the 'FileSystem' provider failed.
  • Explorer This PC spun indefinitely on the VirtIO-FS drive letter (no volume label or capacity bar), and Run went (Not Responding).
  • sc stop VirtioFsSvc timed out with error 1053, while virtiofsd on the host logged zero incoming requests.
path: Debugging Windows 11 guest stalls that look like slow disk I/O

items.title: Cause
items.text: WinFsp.Np sat first in HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\NetworkProvider\Order. While VirtioFsSvc was deadlocked, any process enumerating drives or network providers blocked waiting on it.
path: Debugging Windows 11 guest stalls that look like slow disk I/O

items.title: Fix
items.text:
Disable the service, uninstall WinFsp, and reboot the guest:

sc config VirtioFsSvc start= disabled

After rebooting without the wedged provider, PowerShell 7 and Explorer immediately became responsive. If you need host-to-guest file sharing again later, either reinstall a clean WinFsp build or share the host folder over SMB on the local bridge.
path: Debugging Windows 11 guest stalls that look like slow disk I/O

items.title: 3. Leftover Defender minifilter on a stripped image
path: Debugging Windows 11 guest stalls that look like slow disk I/O

items.title: Symptom and cause
items.text:
Custom stripped Windows builds often remove WinDefend (MsMpEng.exe) while leaving WdFilter attached to every NTFS volume and MpDefenderCoreService running. Check with an elevated prompt:

fltmc
sc query MpDefenderCoreService
path: Debugging Windows 11 guest stalls that look like slow disk I/O

items.title: Fix
items.text:
Stripped guest images only

Only disable leftover Defender drivers on guest images where Defender is already intentionally stripped and broken. Do not apply this on a normal desktop that relies on Microsoft Defender.

Unload/disable the remaining Defender components (WdFilter.sys, WdBoot.sys, WdNisDrv.sys, WdDevFlt.sys) and reboot, then confirm WdFilter no longer appears in fltmc and MpDefenderCoreService is stopped.
path: Debugging Windows 11 guest stalls that look like slow disk I/O

items.title: 4. Stale IPv6 DNS server advertised on the LAN
path: Debugging Windows 11 guest stalls that look like slow disk I/O

items.title: Symptom
items.text:
Every uncached DNS lookup inside Windows stalled for ~24.3 seconds before succeeding:

# Stalled ~24,291 ms via default system resolver
Measure-Command { Resolve-DnsName example.com }

# Completed in ~4 ms when bypassing IPv6 DNS directly
Measure-Command { Resolve-DnsName example.com -Server <lan-dns-ipv4> }

Invoke-WebRequest showed the same ~24-second delay before starting any transfer.
path: Debugging Windows 11 guest stalls that look like slow disk I/O

items.title: Cause
items.text: The OpenWrt router (odhcpd) advertised a stale IPv6 ULA DNS address via dhcp.lan.dns. The local DNS server's DHCPv6 static host entry had no pinned hostid, so after a renewal its ULA suffix drifted (for example, from fd00:0:0:1::10 to fd00:0:0:1::20). Windows preferred the advertised IPv6 DNS address, retried until timeout (~24 seconds), and only then fell back to IPv4.
path: Debugging Windows 11 guest stalls that look like slow disk I/O

items.title: Fix
items.text:
1. Pin the DNS server's IPv6 interface identifier (hostid) on its DHCPv6 static lease in OpenWrt and reload odhcpd:

    uci set dhcp.@host[<index>].hostid='<hostid>'
uci commit dhcp
/etc/init.d/odhcpd reload

  2. Renew the DNS server's DHCPv6 lease (if it does not already hold the pinned address), confirm that the server has acquired the pinned IPv6 address, and verify that its DNS service answers queries on that address before advertising it to LAN clients.

  3. Inspect the current dhcp.lan.dns entries and record every resolver in its current order (whether shown as separate quoted list tokens or a single space-separated string):

    uci show dhcp.lan

  4. Delete dhcp.lan.dns and rebuild it as separate uci add_list entries in the original order, replacing the stale ULA in place with the verified complete IPv6 address (so resolver priority is preserved and any scalar or space-separated value is normalized into valid list entries), then commit and reload odhcpd:

    uci delete dhcp.lan.dns
# Re-add every resolver in its original order, substituting <pinned-ula-address>
# at the position of the stale ULA address:
uci add_list dhcp.lan.dns='<resolver-1-in-original-order>'
uci add_list dhcp.lan.dns='<resolver-2-in-original-order>'
uci commit dhcp
/etc/init.d/odhcpd reload

    Write the complete IPv6 address for <pinned-ula-address>. Because odhcpd accepts hostid values longer than four hex digits, split any longer hostid into 16-bit colon-separated groups (for example, hostid 123456 with prefix fd00:0:0:1::/64 becomes fd00:0:0:1::12:3456).

  5. Re-enable or renew the guest interface and re-test:

    Measure-Command { Resolve-DnsName example.com }

With IPv6 enabled, uncached lookups dropped from ~24,291 ms to ~2.2 ms.
path: Debugging Windows 11 guest stalls that look like slow disk I/O

items.title: 5. Smart App Control Evaluation Mode + missing SmartScreen (2-minute MSI stalls)
path: Debugging Windows 11 guest stalls that look like slow disk I/O

items.title: Symptom
items.text:
Even after VirtIO-FS, Defender leftovers, and DNS were fixed, .msi installers (such as .NET 10 runtime packages and small WiX-based setups) still stalled for ~2 minutes per step, turning routine installs into 20–30+ minute waits.

  • msiexec /V sat idle waiting on msiexec -Embedding.
  • The Windows System event log repeatedly recorded DCOM Event ID 10001 (ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND) trying to activate the SmartScreen COM class {A463FCB9-6B1C-4E0D-A80B-A2CA7999E25D}.
path: Debugging Windows 11 guest stalls that look like slow disk I/O

items.title: Cause
items.text:
This matches the Windows 11 24H2/25H2 Code Integrity / Smart App Control stall documented in microsoft/Windows-Sandbox#68.

Check the current policy state:

Get-ItemProperty -Path "HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\CI\Policy" `
  -Name "VerifiedAndReputablePolicyState"
Value State 0 Off 1 Enforced 2 Evaluation Mode

When VerifiedAndReputablePolicyState is 2 (Evaluation Mode) on an image where SmartScreen has been stripped, Windows still tries to invoke SmartScreen over DCOM during binary and MSI verification. Each attempt waits for the DCOM activation timeout (~2 minutes) before failing over.
path: Debugging Windows 11 guest stalls that look like slow disk I/O

items.title: Fix
items.text:
Set VerifiedAndReputablePolicyState to 0 and refresh Code Integrity policy in place from an elevated PowerShell prompt:

Set-ItemProperty -Path "HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\CI\Policy" `
  -Name "VerifiedAndReputablePolicyState" -Value 0
CiTool.exe --refresh --json

The refresh takes effect immediately without a reboot and persists across restarts. An MSI installer that had been crawling for ~30 minutes finished immediately after running these two lines.
path: Debugging Windows 11 guest stalls that look like slow disk I/O

items.title: 6. Missing SPICE channel and virtio input devices
path: Debugging Windows 11 guest stalls that look like slow disk I/O

items.title: Symptom
items.text: Clipboard sharing between host and guest did not work, and the spice-vdagent installer hung waiting for the agent service to start because the domain XML lacked a SPICE virtio-serial channel.
path: Debugging Windows 11 guest stalls that look like slow disk I/O

items.title: Fix
items.text:
Add the com.redhat.spice.0 channel and virtio input devices to the domain XML (see the full snippet in Looking Glass B7 with IVSHMEM):

<channel type="spicevmc">
  <target type="virtio" name="com.redhat.spice.0"/>
</channel>
<input type="mouse" bus="virtio"/>
<input type="keyboard" bus="virtio"/>

Attach them persistently (virsh edit <domain> or virsh attach-device --config) and perform a full power cycle (shut down and start, not an in-guest reboot) so QEMU exposes the new devices to Windows.
path: Debugging Windows 11 guest stalls that look like slow disk I/O

items.title: Quick triage summary
items.text: Symptom Check Fix Looks like slow disk I/O query-blockstats + block-latency-histogram-set via QMP Verify sub-millisecond host I/O before blaming storage PowerShell InitializeDefaultDrives hang; Explorer This PC spins sc stop VirtioFsSvc times out (1053); WinFsp.Np in NetworkProvider\Order Disable VirtioFsSvc, uninstall WinFsp, reboot Leftover Defender filter on stripped image fltmc shows WdFilter; MpDefenderCoreService running Remove leftover Defender drivers and reboot ~24 s stall on every uncached DNS lookup Resolve-DnsName slow vs -Server <lan-dns-ipv4> fast Pin DNS server IPv6 hostid and update dhcp.lan.dns ~2 min stall per MSI step; DCOM 10001 for {A463FCB9-6B1C-4E0D-A80B-A2CA7999E25D} VerifiedAndReputablePolicyState is 2 with SmartScreen missing Set VerifiedAndReputablePolicyState to 0 and run CiTool.exe --refresh --json No clipboard; spice-vdagent hangs on install Domain XML missing com.redhat.spice.0 Add spicevmc channel + virtio input and cold-boot VM
